content: Nonmetals are a classification of chemical elements based on their distinct physical and chemical properties. In the periodic table, elements are broadly categorized as either metals or nonmetals, with a few elements exhibiting intermediate properties classified as metalloids. The elements commonly identified as nonmetals include: Hydrogen (H) Carbon (C) from Group 14 Nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) from Group 15, also known as the pnictogens Oxygen (O), sulfur (S), and selenium (Se) from Group 16, referred to as the chalcogens All elements in Group 17, collectively called the halogens All elements in Group 18, known as the noble gases The term nonmetal does not have a strict, universally accepted definition but is instead used to describe a general set of behaviors and properties. Nonmetals are typically characterized by the following traits: They are poor conductors of heat and electricity compared to metals. Nonmetals tend to form acidic oxides, in contrast to metals, which generally form basic oxides. In their solid state, nonmetals are dull and brittle, unlike metals, which are lustrous, ductile, and malleable. Nonmetals usually have lower densities than metals. Their melting points and boiling points are significantly lower than those of metals. Nonmetals exhibit high electronegativity. They generally lack luster or shine. Although only 18 elements in the periodic table are typically classified as nonmetals, they play a dominant role in the composition of Earth's crust, atmosphere, and oceans. Furthermore, the bulk of living organisms' tissues is composed almost entirely of nonmetals. Many nonmetals, such as hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, chlorine, bromine, and iodine, exist as diatomic molecules, while others are polyatomic in nature.
